questions.question: should I treat my boots out of box ? Annnnd how often should I treat them ?

hybrid.answer:
**Out of the box: it depends on the leather.** His view comes from his Blundstones and Blundstone's own FAQ, so he hasn't addressed other brands. Blundstone says most of its boots come pretreated [1] and advises against treating them out of the box, because they're already treated [2]. The exception is distressed leathers like Rustic Brown, Crazy Horse and Rustic Black [3]. For those, he strongly recommends treating them [4]. He thinks untreated rustic pairs will likely break down sooner than oiled ones [5].

He changed his mind on this. In his original review, after a puddle test, he took back his claim that the distressed pair wasn't treated [6]. A week later he said that was wrong after reading the FAQ [7].

Two trade-offs he flags:
- Conditioning will darken these leathers [8].
- If you don't want the look to change, he suggests at least looking into silicone or nano sprays, which won't alter the boots as much [9].

**How often: his most recent answer (2022) is "when they need it."** He doesn't follow a schedule: he does it when he feels they need it [10] and admits he probably does too little [11]. His cues:
- If they look or feel dry, or water isn't beading on top, you may need more wax [12].
- Clean them regularly if they're dirty, because dirt wears the leather down faster [13].
- Work in the order clean, condition, wax [14].

His earlier rules of thumb (2019) were that you may have to wax them every month, maybe every week if you're really hard on them [15]. He also said to condition any leather you haven't done in a few months [16].

questions.question: So if I buy the levis 501 shrink to fit will they get tighter after washing?

hybrid.answer:
**Yes. He says the 501 Shrink-to-Fits shrink when you first soak or wash them, so you should buy them bigger.** In his latest take he puts it simply: soak them in the bathtub and they'll shrink, so you should usually go two sizes up [1].

**How much they shrink (2023 comparison):** He sized up two for his STFs [2]. After shrinking, they came out smaller than regular rinsed 501s [3]. He says that if you put them in the dryer they would be a lot smaller from the start [4]. His tip is to avoid very hot water and the dryer, which is how he got a fit he liked [5]. He also guessed that with frequent wear they'd stretch back out to about the same size as rinsed 501s [6].

**Sizing lesson (2021):** He admits it took him four pairs of 501s to accept that Levi's own advice is right [7]. That advice is two sizes up in the waist and two inches more in length [8]. This came up in his review of the $260 LVC 1947 501s, but he framed it as advice for 501s in general.

**His first pair (2019):** He ignored Levi's sizing advice. After the hot soak the waist was very tight, and he found they'd slimmed mainly through the waist [9], while the length barely changed [10]. A week later the waist and upper thighs had stretched enough that he could wear a belt [11]. One caveat: he had tapered the legs himself before that follow-up, so the slimmer lower leg wasn't from shrinking [12].

In short, they'll get tighter, mostly in the waist, and then loosen somewhat with wear. How much they shrink depends on how hot you wash and whether you use the dryer.

questions.question: Why do you cuff your jeans?

**The exception, with boots (Nov 2019):** In his L.L.Bean boot review he says he always used to cuff his jeans but had come to prefer them pulled down over his boots [3]. He thinks that tones down a loud statement boot. For a more workwear look with Bean boots, he suggests a 7 to 7.5 inch leg opening worn over the boot [4].

questions.question: So do you prefer [the Red Wing 3335s] over the 1907s?

hybrid.answer:
**Mostly yes, though by 2023 he was less sure, and he decided to get rid of the 3335s anyway.**

**Most recent view (Sept 2023):** He noted that he is on record calling the 3335s his favourite Red Wings, and said "they still might be but they probably not" [1]. He added that the 875s, 1907s and Iron Rangers "all have their own characteristics" he really likes [1]. He still values the 3335s for their stitch-down construction, lighter weight and nimbler feel, which make them easier for walking or a light hike [1]. Even so, they were on his list of boots to go when he was cutting down his collection [1].

**Earlier view (Oct 2022):** He clearly preferred the 3335s. He called them his favourite boots he'd ever had and said they beat the 1907s, the 875s and his Blundstones [2]. His reasons:
- **They suit how he uses boots.** He's going on hikes and walks in the woods, not doing heritage work. He sees the 3335s as "a dramatically better all-around boot," and he thinks they look way cooler [2][3].
- **The sole.** He prefers the 3335's Vibram mini lug sole, which he doesn't expect to break down as fast as the crepe soles on the 875s and 1907s [4].

He didn't claim they win on everything:
- **Toughness.** He said the 1907s and 875s are more beefily built, so if you need a tough boot, the 3335s probably aren't the ones [2].
- **Construction.** Because the 3335s use only a single stitch, he didn't think their stitch-down construction made them "infinitely better" than the 1907s or 875s [5].

**Context on the 1907 (Sept 2021):** Before the 3335 review, he argued the 1907 was the best Red Wing moc toe. His reasoning was value: for about $10 more than the 875 you get a storm welt, a removable leather footbed and leather laces [6].

questions.question: How does the made in England boot stack up to Solovairs? [Dr. Martens]

hybrid.answer:
**In his view, Solovair beats Made in England Dr. Martens on value and build.** In his 2022 Dr. Martens review he says that if you want pure value and a better-built boot, Solovair is the pick. He loves Solovair [1], and he points out that it's actually cheaper than Made in England Docs [2]. He mentions in that video that he isn't sponsored by either brand [3].

**Why he favors Solovair:**
- **Leather and midsoles are roughly equal.** He grants that Made in England Docs have better leather and midsoles than regular Docs, but thinks both are probably on par with Solovair [4].
- **Solovair has a shank.** Their boots have one [5], which he says makes them more comfortable over long periods. Docs have no shank, so they're easier to break in at first, while Solovairs are tougher to break in but more comfortable down the line [6].
- **Easier resoling.** Solovairs are Goodyear welted in a more conventional way, so they're easier to resole [7].
- **Same look, from the original maker.** He notes Solovair is a smaller company and one of the original makers of Doc Martens, and says their 8-eye derby boot is essentially the exact same boot [8].
- **What you pay for with Made in England.** He feels the extra cost, about a third of the boot's price, mostly buys the "Made in England" label itself [9]. He even says that with an unlimited budget he'd choose the regular 1460s over the Made in England pair [10].

**The one reason he'd choose Made in England:** Solovair doesn't do the yellow stitching. If that matters to you and you want the highest quality, you'd have to get the Made in England Docs [11].

**A caveat about his own Solovairs:** after eight wears, a back tab ripped off one boot and a lace snapped. He believes it's a manufacturing defect and had contacted Solovair [12]. The transcripts don't say how that turned out.

**His later take (2023):** In his newer video he compared Made in England Docs with the Made in Thailand ones, not with Solovair, so he didn't revisit the Solovair matchup. His view of the Made in England line stayed about the same. Objectively, he says they're probably not worth the extra $90 [13]. Still, if you're a big fan who wants boots made like the old Docs, you have to go Made in England [14]. As things stand, he thinks you have to be a "mega fan" to buy them [15].

questions.question: Hi, I am going on a 4 day hike and I am wondering if I can use my blundstone for them, what do you think?

hybrid.answer:
**Short answer:** He hasn't talked about multi-day hikes specifically, but his experience suggests Blundstones can handle hiking with some caveats, mainly the lack of ankle support.

**What he found after a year of wear (2020, his most recent take):**
- He went on a lot of hikes and climbed a lot of mountains in his pair [1]. He says they're "not good boots for mountaining apparently" because they don't have good ankle support [2].
- They held up well on hikes in Maine, though they got scuffed [3]. There were more scuffs than he expected, which he puts down to kicking rocks on descents [4].
- On water, he stood in a pond in boots that hadn't been treated for a year. He concluded you should be fine crossing a brook or stream or standing in mud for a bit [5], though he wouldn't stand in still water in them for long [6].
- He also brings up break-in in that video [7]. According to the video's notes, he got blisters once he started running and walking long distances in them, and they stopped after two to three weeks. If yours are new, a 4-day trip could be rough.

**Care matters:**
- In his original review, he recommends them only if you'll keep them treated, and says to buy them "knowing that you'll have to take care of them" [8].
- He later corrected himself about distressed leathers. Citing Blundstone's FAQ, he notes that styles like rustic brown and Crazy Horse don't carry the same pretreatment as finished, oiled leather [9]. If yours are one of those, conditioning them before a wet trip fits his advice.

**Context:** He owns separate boots he calls hiking boots, his Keens [10]. He describes Blundstones more as a versatile boot that can "kind of go anywhere" [11].

**What's missing:** He doesn't address multi-day treks, carrying a heavy pack or long daily mileage. So his take is: fine for hiking if your pair is broken in and kept treated, but expect weak ankle support on rough or mountainous terrain.

full.answer:
**Short version:** The Iron Snail has hiked in his Blundstones and says they held up, but he has never talked about a multi-day trip like a 4-day hike. His main caveat is that they lack ankle support.

**What he found hiking in them**
- In his one-year review (2020), he says he went on a lot of hikes and climbed mountains in them [1]. He also says they're "not good boots for mountaining" because they don't have good ankle support [2].
- They got scuffed on rocky descents but held up well [3]. He notes there were more scuffs than he expected [4].
- Overall he calls them decent for work but "not anything incredible" [5]. He sees them more as a good all-rounder for walks around town than a specialised tool [6].
- **Blisters:** even after hiking in them, he got big break-in blisters once he started walking long distances on a track in them. These stopped after two to three weeks [7]. If yours aren't well broken in, keep that in mind for long days.

**Water**
- After a year without retreating them, he stood in a pond and concluded they're fine for crossing a brook or stream or standing in mud for a bit [8]. In his first review he said he wouldn't stand in water for hours, though [9].
- By 2023 he called his pair "probably my most water resistant boots" after years of hard wear [10].
- He stresses that this depends on upkeep: buy them knowing you'll have to take care of them [11]. Re-wax if the leather looks dry or isn't beading water [12].

**What's missing:** He hasn't addressed carrying a heavy pack, multiple consecutive days on trail, or Blundstones specifically for backpacking. So whether they're right for your 4-day trip isn't something he has judged. Based on what he has said, the ankle-support caveat and being broken in and freshly treated are the things he'd flag.

- His one complaint is aesthetic: the 5x1 rib knit on the cuffs, hem and collar. He'd prefer 2x1 or 1x1 [10].

questions.question: How does Uniqlo compare to The Front General Store,  Proclub, and Hanes? ie what is the best budget shirt?

hybrid.answer:
**Short answer:** In his most recent roundup, The Iron Snail calls Uniqlo the best pure budget shirt: at $20 it's "probably the best t-shirt that you can get bar none for the price" [1]. Front General Store is his step-up pick, a $40 shirt made in Japan [2]. He has praised Pro Club and Hanes too, but only in an older video, and he never put them head-to-head with Uniqlo.

**Uniqlo (his go-to bargain)**
- **September 2025:** He calls it "your starter t-shirt," while noting the fabric is open-ended and "kind of rough" [3]. If you're taller or wider, he points you to Muji instead. It costs about $4–5 more but is significantly longer and wider [3].
- **June 2025:** He said the price-to-quality ratio is "insane" and that you get a bound neck collar that doesn't wiggle much [4]. He wears the black one all the time [4].
- In that same video, he rated Bronson (at $29) and Bravestar Selvage (at $32) as "slightly above Uniclo" on value [5].
- **July 2024:** He already said the Uniqlo heavyweight crew "may be" the best bargain t-shirt, partly because it has the bound, ribbed collar he likes [6].

**Front General Store (the upgrade)**
- **September 2025:** He describes it as a $40, 100% made-in-Japan shirt with "great proportions, great feel" [2]. He recalls it as a previous winner, maybe second place, tied with Asket [2].
- **June 2025:** He called it "still really good" [7].
- **August 2024:** He said it might knock the most-voted shirt off the list [8]. He thinks the yarn is open-ended but sanded for some softness [8].
  - Shrinkage was 1.2% in width and 0% in length, because it's pre-washed.
  - He gave it 6/10 for softness.
  - His verdict: for an upgrade under $40, it's "one of the best shirts that you could possibly get" [8].

**Pro Club (August 2024 only)**
- It feels like an "old school American shirt" and is the roughest shirt on that list, which he's sure uses open-ended yarns [9].
- He still likes "everything about it," including the high neck hole with Lycra [9].
- It shrank 2.78% in width and 6.86% in length, and he gave it 4/10 for softness [9].

**Hanes (August 2024 only)**
- The Beefy-T is "much much softer than the Pro Club" and lighter weight, with a similar fit but slightly lower armholes [9].
- He calls it "your classic $10 great shirt" [10].
- It shrank 1.45% in width and 6.73% in length, and he gave it 7/10 for softness [10].

**Bottom line**
- **Cheapest strong pick:** Uniqlo.
- **Bigger builds:** Muji.
- **Made in Japan around $40:** Front General Store.
- **Pro Club vs. Hanes:** Pro Club is the tougher, rougher shirt; Hanes is the softer one. Both shrank a lot in length in his tests.

Other value picks he has mentioned include House of Blanks at $35 [11] and Bronson, which he admits he forgot to include in the latest list [11].

**I can't tell which jacket "this" is**, so I can't give a head-to-head pick. Below is what The Iron Snail has said about the Flint and Tinder and the two jackets he most directly sets beside it. He has never judged any of them specifically as a windbreaker.

**Flint and Tinder Waxed Trucker (Huckberry)**
- In his 2025 ranking he says it's for "everyone" [1]. It's a lighter weight, so it's comfortable [1]. It's lined, so you don't get wax on your skin [2]. He calls $300 for a lined, US-made jacket in Martexin fabric hard to beat [2].
- That segment was in a **Huckberry-sponsored video**. He points out he praised the jacket many times before the sponsorship [3].
- In his 2023 guide (not Huckberry-sponsored), he looked at the 7 oz unlined version. He said it can be worn when it's a little warmer [4]. He pictured its wearer putting it on when it's raining, with a hat [5]. His one con was the lack of lining [6].

**Barbour (Bedale)**
This is the one he ties most closely to rain.
- In 2025 he says it's not a designated rain jacket, but its fabric is the lightest of the bunch [7]. He says you could wear it any time of year and be comfortable [8]. He loves the throat latch and finds the storm cuffs helpful in bad weather [9].
- In his 2021 review, his new Bedale didn't leak in a shower test [10]. He notes the storm flap stops water running through the zipper [11].
- He says thornproof finishes add wind and water resistance [12].
- He stresses that water resistance depends on the state of the wax [13]. Waxed jackets are not waterproof, but they are very water resistant when properly treated [10].

**Devium Overdrive**
He says if you like the Flint and Tinder, put this one on your list [14]. He adds it won't be too hot or too cold wherever you live [14].

If you tell me which jacket you're looking at, I can say what, if anything, he said about it versus the Flint and Tinder.
